opus-5.5.text:
I think there are two related but distinct limitations, and they come from the same root.

For world modeling, large language models learn an extremely rich statistical picture of how people *talk about* the world. That gets you surprisingly far, because a lot of structure is encoded in language. But it's not the same as having a compact, mechanistic model. When I look at what's happening inside these networks, the representations are often a patchwork of heuristics. They work well within the distribution of the training data, but they don't necessarily compress into the kind of simple, generalizable laws a physicist would write down. A model can predict the next sentence about a falling ball very well without internally representing something like F = ma in a clean, reusable way. So when you push it into regimes that are genuinely new, where you need to extrapolate from principles rather than interpolate from examples, it tends to break in ways that are hard to anticipate.

For Auto Research, that limitation becomes even more important. Science isn't only about retrieving or recombining what's known. A big part of it is noticing that something is surprising, that the current theory doesn't fit, and then being willing to sit with that discomfort until you find a new abstraction. Current LLMs are trained to produce plausible continuations, so they're biased toward the consensus, toward what sounds right. Real discovery often requires the opposite: taking an idea that sounds wrong and testing it carefully. There's also the question of taste. Knowing which problem is worth working on, which simplification is the right one, which result is actually interesting. That's very hard to learn from text alone, because the text mostly records the successful end products, not the messy process and the many dead ends.

That said, I don't think these limitations are fundamental in a mystical sense. They point to things we can work on. One direction I care about is interpretability and building models whose internal structure is more transparent and closer to symbolic or mechanistic forms. That's part of the motivation behind things like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. If a model's internals are closer to formulas, it's easier for humans to collaborate with it, check it, and extract actual scientific insight. Another direction is coupling LLMs with tools and with real feedback from experiments or simulations, so they're not only reasoning in language but are grounded in the consequences of their hypotheses.

So in my view, LLMs are already very useful research assistants: they lower the cost of literature search, coding, and trying ideas. But the step from assistant to genuine autonomous scientist requires better world models, better grounding, and something like scientific taste. Those are open problems, and honestly, that's what makes this period exciting.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that large language models are extraordinarily good at compressing what humans have already written down, and that's both their superpower and their ceiling when it comes to world modeling and research.

Let me start with world modeling. A language model learns the statistics of text about the world, not the world itself. Text is a very lossy, very biased projection. Nobody writes down "I dropped the cup and it fell at 9.8 meters per second squared" a billion times, and nobody writes down the ten thousand small things that didn't happen. So the model ends up with something that looks like a world model, because it can describe physics beautifully in words, but when you push it to actually simulate, to predict a trajectory, to keep a consistent state over many steps, it starts to drift. It's a bit like someone who has read every textbook about swimming but never been in water. From the outside the vocabulary is perfect. Inside, there's no grounding.

Coming from physics, the way I'd put it is that LLMs are good at pattern matching and bad at conservation laws. A physical world model has constraints that hold no matter what: energy, momentum, consistency across time. A language model has no hard constraints. It has soft priors. If the context nudges it, it will happily violate things that should be invariant, and it won't even notice, because nothing in its training objective ever penalized inconsistency across long horizons.

On Auto Research, I'm actually both excited and a little worried. The exciting part is that a lot of science is, frankly, boring in a mechanical sense. Literature search, writing boilerplate code, running sweeps, generating candidate hypotheses that are recombinations of known ideas. LLMs are great at all of that, and that's not nothing. That's maybe eighty percent of a graduate student's week.

But the part of research that matters, the part that changes a field, is usually the moment someone notices that the question itself is wrong. That the thing everyone assumed was fixed is actually a variable. I don't think current models do that well, and I think there's a structural reason. They are trained to be plausible. Research breakthroughs are, almost by definition, the implausible thing that turns out to be true. If you optimize for what sounds reasonable given everything humans have said so far, you're optimizing against novelty in a subtle way.

There's a second limitation that I think is underrated: taste. When I'm doing research, most of my time is spent deciding what not to do. Which of these fifty ideas is worth three months of my life. That judgment comes from having been wrong many times and feeling it. Models don't have that feedback loop yet. They generate twenty hypotheses with equal confidence and no sense of which one is actually interesting. So in practice, an automated research pipeline today tends to produce a lot of output that is locally correct and globally uninteresting.

And then there's the verification problem. In math or physics, a wrong answer is cheap to produce and expensive to check. If the model is doing both the generation and the evaluation, you get this closed loop where it convinces itself. I've seen systems write a derivation, write a check for the derivation, and both are wrong in the same direction. Humans do this too, to be fair, but we have a community of other humans who are motivated to prove us wrong. The model doesn't have an adversary unless you build one in.

So where does that leave me? I don't think the answer is that LLMs can't do science. I think the answer is that the bottleneck has shifted. It used to be that generating ideas and code was slow. Now that's fast, and the bottleneck is grounding and judgment. The interesting work, at least the work I care about, is building systems where the model is forced to interact with something that pushes back: a simulator, an experiment, a formal verifier, a structured representation that makes inconsistency visible. Something with actual constraints, not just more text.

My own bias is toward interpretability and structure, so I'd put it this way: I'd rather have a smaller model that knows what it doesn't know than a larger one that's fluent about everything. For world modeling and for research, the thing we're missing is not more knowledge. It's the ability to be surprised, and then to take the surprise seriously.

astra-6.text:
I think we should separate two questions: can a model describe the world convincingly, and can it build a model of the world that helps us discover something new? Those are related, but they’re not the same.

A language model learns from descriptions of the world. That gives it a lot of useful structure, but a description leaves things out. In physics, for example, you want to know which variables matter, what assumptions you’re making, and whether a relationship still holds when you change the conditions. A model can produce a very plausible explanation without having those pieces consistently connected. The real test is whether it makes predictions that survive experiments, especially outside the situations represented in its training data.

For automated research, that distinction becomes very important. Generating a hypothesis or writing code is only part of research. You also have to choose a useful question, design a test that could show your idea is wrong, and recognize when the result means you should change your assumptions. If the same system proposes an idea and judges it only by how persuasive the explanation sounds, it can get stuck reinforcing its own mistakes.

So I see a lot of potential when language models are connected to reliable feedback: simulations, mathematical checks, experiments. In a narrowly defined problem where you can evaluate progress clearly, automation can go quite far. The harder case is open-ended research, where even deciding what counts as progress is part of the discovery.

The limitation isn’t simply that models need more knowledge. It’s whether they can turn knowledge into a cycle of prediction, testing, and revision. That’s the capability I would want to measure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish two things: being able to describe the world and being able to build a model that lets you predict and intervene in it. Large language models are very good at learning patterns from descriptions. But if a model can explain a physical phenomenon fluently, that alone doesn’t tell us whether it has captured the underlying mechanism. A stronger test is whether it can predict what happens under new conditions, identify when its assumptions fail, and update its understanding from experiments.

That matters especially for automated research. Research is not just generating plausible ideas or producing a paper-shaped output. You need to choose a useful question, formulate a hypothesis, design a test that could prove you wrong, and interpret the result. Language models can help with many of those steps, particularly when the task has clear feedback, such as running code or checking a mathematical argument. But when the feedback is ambiguous, they can produce convincing explanations without actually resolving the uncertainty.

There’s also a problem with the objective. If you ask a system to improve a benchmark, it may become very effective at improving that benchmark. Whether that produces new scientific understanding is a separate question. Often the difficult part of research is deciding what is worth measuring in the first place.

So I wouldn’t say language models cannot do research or cannot learn world models. I would say that language fluency is insufficient evidence for either. The promising direction is to connect them to experiments, explicit models, and reliable verification—and evaluate whether they discover something that continues to hold up outside the setting where it was found.
